title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Maya Rodriguez
content:
Overview:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s security and compliance controls for Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) requirements, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and the process for managing risk and exceptions. It is intended for security, engineering, product, and compliance teams responsible for implementing and maintaining controls across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Objectives:
- Define minimum required controls and owners.
- Provide operational procedures for logging, evidence collection, incident handling, and exception approvals.
- Align retention and residency settings with legal, contractual, and regulatory obligations.
- Provide a repeatable exceptions process with compensating controls.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Summary:
Redwood uses centralized RBAC for cloud control plane components, platform consoles, and internal tooling. Authentication is SSO-first with strong MFA requirements and short lifetime service tokens for machine identities.

Scope:
- Admin consoles (Console UI, admin APIs)
- Internal services (deployment orchestration, observability, billing)
- Customer-facing control plane where applicable (Dedicated/private admin endpoints)

Roles and Permissions (canonical list):
- Security Admin: full access to security controls, audit exports, and exception approvals. Owned by Security.
- Platform Admin: manage infrastructure, deployments, and capacity. Owned by Eng-Infra.
- SRE: incident response, runbook execution, limited config changes. Owned by Eng-SRE.
- Dev: standard development access to code and deployment pipelines. No access to production secrets.
- Support: read-only access to customer metadata as required; escalated write-only for customer troubleshooting via controlled workflows.

Policy and Standards:
- Principle of least privilege applied to all roles. All new roles and role changes must go through a documented approval and justification in the access-request system.
- SSO with SCIM provisioning: Okta (primary). All user access must be provisioned/deprovisioned via SCIM where supported.
- MFA requirement: MFA enabled for all human users; hardware keys preferred for administrators.
- Service accounts: short-lived tokens (max 7 days) for non-human identities; long-lived credentials require explicit exception and key-management justification.
- Periodic access review: quarterly reviews for all privileged roles; owner must attest in the access-review tool.

Enforcement and Controls:
- Access enforcement for internal APIs via IAM policies and service mesh mutual TLS.
- Secrets stored in KMS-backed vaults (AWS KMS + HashiCorp Vault or HSM in Private deployments).
- Just-in-time (JIT) elevation supported for emergency tasks: JIT grants are time-limited, logged, require approval, and are audited.

Ownership:
- Security team: policy owner and approver for exceptions.
- Eng-Infra: implementation and enforcement of IAM and provisioning.

2) Audit Logging

Logging Coverage:
- Authentication & authorization events (login, SSO lifecycle, token issuance, token revocation).
- Administrative actions (policy changes, role assignments, KMS rotations).
- Data access events for sensitive datasets (views, downloads, exports).
- System events: deployments, scaling events, configuration changes.
- Incident-related actions: containment activities, user revocations.

Log Transport and Storage:
- Centralized logging cluster (ELK/Opensearch) for infrastructure logs; audit sink to an append-only WORM storage for compliance exports.
- Logs are forwarded to a secure long-term archive (S3 with object lock for WORM where required by contract).
- For Private deployments, logs may be directed to customer-managed sinks per contract; Redwood provides a guidance template for log schema and retention.

Retention and Integrity:
- Default retention: 365 days in hot storage, 3+ years in cold archive for customer-sensitive events depending on contract/regulation.
- Integrity: logs are signed and hashed using HMAC/SHA-256 at write time; periodic integrity scans against stored checksums.
- Access to raw audit logs is limited to Security and SRE on a need-to-know basis and governed by an approval workflow.

Alerting and Monitoring:
- High-risk events (privileged role creation, mass data export, unexpected token issuance) produce high-priority alerts to PagerDuty SecOps channels.
- Baseline detection: anomalies in admin activity are auto-triaged and produce incidents when thresholds are crossed (e.g., >5 role changes in 1 hour by same principal).

3) Data Residency & Retention

Residency Principles:
- Customer data residency is honored per customer configuration: data at rest is stored only in selected regions for Hosted and Dedicated customers.
- Private deployments operate under customer network and residency constraints.

Retention Baselines (default unless overridden by contract):
- Non-sensitive logs & telemetry: 90 days (hot), 1 year (cold).
- Audit logs & security events: 365 days (hot), 3 years (archive).
- Backups of customer data: 90-day snapshot cycle with encrypted snapshots retained per contract (default 1 year).
- Model artifacts (open models): retained per product policy; customer-provided models follow contract terms.

Encryption & Key Management:
- At-rest encryption for all data using KMS-managed keys. For Hosted, Redwood-managed KMS; Dedicated/Private support customer-managed KMS.
- Keys rotated at minimum annually; emergency rotations documented and executed via runbook.

Data Deletion Requests:
- Process owner: Customer Success for customer-facing deletion requests; Security and Eng-Infra for system-wide deletion requests.
- Deletion verification: cryptographic deletion or overwrite is documented; verification artifacts (deletion ticket, audit log entries) stored in evidence workflow.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Software Development Lifecycle)

Principles:
- Security gate checks integrated into CI/CD pipelines with automated static analysis, secret scanning, dependency vulnerability scanning, and SCA for third-party components.
- Mandatory code review for all changes; privileged code paths require two approvers and a security review for high-risk changes.

Requirements and Controls:
- Pre-merge checks: unit tests, linting, SAST, secret-scan, SBOM generation.
- Build artifacts: signed and reproducible where possible; build provenance recorded for release.
- Release approvals: major/minor release requires a release checklist that includes SLO/SLR (service level readiness), security review, and deployment rollback plan.
- Penetration tests: annual third-party pen test for production environments and additional tests for major changes.

Developer Training and Ownership:
- Secure coding training required annually for all engineers.
- Threat modeling: required for new services handling sensitive data. Modeled threats and mitigations must be recorded in the design doc.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Incident Classification:
- Sev 1 (Security Emergency): active compromise, data exfiltration, or production-wide availability impact caused by security event. Immediate P0 response and executive escalation.
- Sev 2: targeted compromise affecting subset of systems or customers. Standard SecOps response.
- Sev 3: low-impact security issues requiring remediation and review.

Initial Triage and Containment (high-level procedure):
1. Detection & Triage: Alert reviewed by on-call SRE + SecOps; assign incident lead.
2. Containment: Isolate affected services, rotate potentially compromised credentials, and apply temporary ACLs or firewall blocks.
3. Forensic Preservation: Capture snapshots of affected hosts, preserve logs in WORM archive, and collect memory images if required.
4. Communication: Notify internal stakeholders per incident comms plan; customer notification handled by Customer Success following legal review for incidents affecting customer data.
5. Recovery: Execute validated rollback or patch and monitor for re-occurrence.
6. Post-Incident Review: 72-hour timeline for incident blameless postmortem draft; security and SRE to publish follow-up actions and owners.

Evidence and Chain-of-Custody:
- All forensic artifacts must be cataloged in the incident ticket with hash sums, storage location, and access controls.
- Evidence retention per incident classification: Sev1 artifacts retained for minimum 3 years unless legal requires longer retention.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose:
Provide reproducible evidence for auditors and contractual obligations (ISO, SOC2, regional regulations).

Evidence Types & Owners:
- Policy artifacts: documented policies (this doc), owner: Security.
- Access lists: SCIM provisioning exports and quarterly access-review attestations, owner: Eng-Infra.
- Configuration snapshots: Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform) state exports for a given date, owner: Eng-Infra.
- Log exports: signed audit log exports with checksums, owner: Security/SRE.
- Incident artifacts: postmortems, forensic artifacts, remediation tickets, owner: Security.

Workflow Steps (standard audit request):
1. Request intake: Compliance or external auditor files request in the compliance ticketing project with required scope and date range.
2. Triage & scoping: Security triages request, identifies owners for each evidence type, and produces an evidence plan (timeline 10 business days standard).
3. Collection: Owners provide signed artifacts and metadata. All artifacts include a short provenance statement describing how item was generated.
4. Packaging: Evidence packaged into a read-only archive (WORM) with manifest and checksums.
5. Delivery & attestation: Security delivers archive to auditor/customer and records delivery in the compliance tracker.

SLAs for Evidence Requests:
- Standard evidence request: 10 business days.
- Expedited request: 3 business days (requires approval from Security Director and may incur costs).

7) Risk & Exceptions Process

When to request an exception:
- Business need requires deviation from policy (legacy integration, long-lived service key).
- Technical constraints in a Private deployment where required tooling is unavailable.

Exception Workflow:
1. Submit exception request in exception system with: scope, duration, rationale, risk assessment, and proposed compensating controls.
2. Security reviews request; may consult Legal or Privacy for regulatory impacts.
3. Approval matrix: Security Manager can approve medium-risk exceptions for up to 90 days; Security Director approves high-risk exceptions; Board or CISO required for multi-year or enterprise-impacting exceptions.
4. Mitigation and monitoring: every approved exception must have compensating controls and increased monitoring (e.g., enhanced logging, daily attestations).
5. Renewal & closure: exceptions auto-expire; owner must renew with fresh justification.

Compensating Controls (examples):
- If long-lived credentials required: enforce IP-restricted usage, daily rotation via automation, and additional anomaly detection.
- If cannot route logs to central archive in Private deployment: require local WORM archive with signed manifests and quarterly evidence transfers to Redwood’s compliance repository under NDA.

Metrics & Reporting:
- Quarterly exception inventory maintained by Security (owner, risk rating, expiry, compensating controls).
- Monthly dashboard: number of active exceptions, age distribution, and incident correlation.

Owners and Contacts:

- Operational owners: Eng-Infra (IAM provisioning), Eng-SRE (logging & monitoring), Customer Success (customer notifications)
- Escalation: Security Director, Legal Counsel, and CTO as per incident comms matrix.

- 2025-11-12: Initial baseline published.
- 2026-02-20: Updated retention baselines and evidence SLAs; clarified exception approvals.
